answer.answer:
Healthline contrasts two meat-free, plant-forward eating patterns for healthier eating: the VEGETARIAN diet and the PESCATARIAN diet (Healthline defines a pescatarian as someone who eats a vegetarian diet but also eats fish/seafood; fish is animal flesh, so vegetarians exclude it, while pescatarians allow it). Both are far more flexible than a vegan diet.

SIMILARITIES (both good for eating healthier): Both exclude red meat and poultry (beef, pork, chicken, etc.) and emphasize nutrient-dense plant foods (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes). Both are linked to lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, and both are more sustainable than meat-heavy diets. Both commonly include eggs and dairy if desired.

PESCATARIAN DIET — plant-based foods plus fish/seafood; may include dairy and eggs. Pros: more flexible and easier to follow than vegetarian/vegan, with more restaurant options; adds nutrients plant foods often lack — omega-3s (EPA/DHA from oily fish like salmon, sardines), vitamin B12, vitamin D, iodine, zinc, selenium, and lean protein. Research cited: pescatarian women gained ~2.5 fewer lb per year than meat eaters; pescatarians had lower diabetes risk (4.8% vs 7.6% for omnivores); rare-meat-eaters/pescatarians had 22% lower risk of dying from heart disease. Cons: larger fish can contain mercury/other toxins — FDA advises young children and people who are pregnant/nursing or of childbearing age to avoid tilefish, swordfish, shark and king mackerel, and limit albacore/yellowfin tuna to no more than one palm-sized serving/week (light tuna, 2–3 servings/week, is fine).

VEGETARIAN DIET — excludes all meat, fish and poultry; usually includes dairy/eggs (lacto-ovo). Pros: better overall diet quality and higher intake of fiber, vitamin C, vitamin E and magnesium; weight loss (a review of 12 studies found ~4.5 lb more loss over 18 weeks, and in a 6-month study of 74 people with type 2 diabetes it was nearly twice as effective as a low-calorie diet; lower BMI in ~61,000 adults); possibly lower cancer risk (breast, colon, rectum); better blood-sugar control and ~53% lower diabetes risk in one study; improved cholesterol/LDL. Cons: needs planning to meet B12, iron and omega-3s — it only supplies ALA omega-3 (from walnuts/flaxseed), which the body converts to EPA/DHA poorly.

HEALTHLINE'S BOTTOM LINE: A pescatarian diet is a healthy choice and offers 'more flexibility and some additional nutrition compared to a standard vegetarian diet' — the seafood supplies EPA/DHA omega-3s (good for brain and heart) plus vitamin B12, vitamin D, iodine and lean protein that strict vegetarian/vegan diets can lack, so nutrient needs are easier to meet. A well-planned vegetarian diet is also healthy (linked to weight loss, better blood sugar, cholesterol and lower chronic-disease risk) but requires more care to cover B12/iron/omega-3s. For eating healthier, the pescatarian diet is the easier-to-follow option that adds heart- and brain-friendly omega-3s, provided you choose fish wisely to limit mercury; vegetarians can get similar benefits with planning, while a flexitarian approach is a more flexible middle ground.

Mediterranean: plant-forward with fish/seafood at least twice a week, generous olive oil, limited poultry/eggs/dairy and occasional red meat, no calorie counting; may help manage weight, support heart health and reduce diabetes risk; frequently ranked among the top diets for heart health. Verdict: both are healthy and nearly interchangeable - the pescatarian diet is essentially the Mediterranean pattern minus poultry/red meat, so the Mediterranean diet is the broader, best-studied and easiest to sustain, while a whole-foods pescatarian diet (not processed/junk-food pescatarian) is equally heart-healthy; vary fish to limit mercury.
